AI is rapidly changing the processes and documents used by librarians and media specialists, but on-site judgment and professional experience remain human responsibilities. This page explains the specific effects and response paths.
It does not suit people who dislike quiet, cannot tolerate repetition, or become impatient with others. Librarians frequently answer questions and run programs, making indifference a poor fit.
A common path is: start as an assistant or volunteer, become a librarian, manage a collection independently, lead a branch, then become a library director or subject librarian.
This work suits calm, organized, empathetic people. If delivering the right resource to the right person feels like the right standard, the field can be stable.

Librarians and media collections specialists lead collection development and reader services, coordinating acquisition, cataloging, systems, and programs. They use classification and research methods to support circulation and follow up on reader needs.

paragraphs: In the morning, acquire new materials and verify classification and holdings. At midday, discuss needs with readers and adjust reading lists. Before a program, walk through the process and revise it several times. Spend the afternoon preparing reading guidance and integrating digital resources, then organize circulation data for the following week's programs.

In short, they place knowledge within readers' reach. They acquire and catalog materials, run programs, guide readers, integrate digital resources, and promote reading, combining analysis and empathy on the frontline of knowledge services.

U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) data show about 142,100 librarians and media collections specialists employed in 2024, projected to reach 144,500 by 2034. That is a net increase of about 2,400 jobs, with roughly 13,500 annual openings. Median annual pay is about $64,300 in 2026 (BLS OOH, 2026).

AI will not replace librarians, but it will reduce routine roles. Research and automated cataloging accelerate organization, shifting librarians from managing books toward selection, reader guidance, program design, and digital integration. Mechanical cataloging roles face pressure, while people with sound selection and guidance skills become more valuable.

paragraphs: A 6/10 score places this occupation at moderate AI exposure in knowledge services. Systems accelerate routine cataloging, while people retain responsibility for selection and reading guidance.

Moderate-high exposure does not mean high risk. AI replaces mechanical cataloging tasks, not selection and reader-guidance roles. Librarians who choose well and engage readers become scarcer as productivity rises; shelving-only roles face the greatest pressure.
Build selection and digital skills from a library and information science foundation. Pure cataloging is shrinking in the AI era, so develop reading-guidance skills early.
Advance from managing books to selecting resources plus leading programs. Learn data skills and pursue subject-librarian work.
Emphasize service and program experience, clearly identifying the collections you have worked with. Institutions value steadiness and warmth.
Do not hire on credentials alone. Look for the ability to guide readers; staff who engage readers effectively merit stable professional roles.
